analysis.title: GraphRAG-Bench medical-domain generation quality and task-complexity results
analysis.summary: Page presents Table 1 and Figure 3 from GraphRAG-Bench (Medical domain), comparing LightRAG, HippoRAG 2, and RAGU. Table 1 reports Answer Correctness (AC), Coverage (Cov), and Faithfulness (Faith), all ×100. Best values are: HippoRAG 2 with Qwen2.5-7B for Fact Retrieval AC (72.7); HippoRAG 2 with Meno-Lite-0.1 for Complex Reasoning AC (68.4) and Contextual Summarization AC (65.0); RAGU with Qwen2.5-7B for Contextual Summarization Cov (73.2) and Creative Generation Faith (35.1); and RAGU with Meno-Lite-0.1 for Creative Generation AC (59.0) and Cov (57.4). Figure 3 uses Meno-Lite-0.1 and gpt-4o-mini: in Answer Correctness, RAGU trails HippoRAG 2 on Fact Retrieval (54.2 vs. 72.4), nearly closes the gap on Contextual Summarize (64.1 vs. 65.0), and leads Creative Generation (59.0 vs. 56.9). Evidence Recall values for LightRAG/HippoRAG 2/RAGU are Fact Retrieval 76.1/75.6/82.4, Complex Reasoning 71.3/66.7/74.5, Contextual Summarize 70.2/71.8/74.8, and Creative Generation 59.9/36.2/53.1. Section 3.3, “Multi-Hop QA Results,” argues that answer format strongly affects overlap-based metrics: under a terse controlled format, RAGU reaches BioASQ AC 72.9 vs. HippoRAG 2 at 72.4 and narrows the 2WikiMultiHopQA gap from −19.3 percentage points to −5.5 points (58.0 vs. 63.5), while HippoRAG 2 retains a lead on MuSiQue (54.4 vs. 40.1).

3.3 Multi-Hop QA Results

These benchmarks are pure factoid QA with short gold answers, for which answer format strongly affects overlap-based metrics. We therefore report two answer-generation protocols (Table 2): (a) each system’s default verbose prompt, and (b) a terse prompt that forces a single direct answer. HippoRAG 2 appears in both panels unchanged because its default prompt already emits terse output, making it a format anchor; NaiveRAG is RAGU’s NaiveSearchEngine and therefore shares our generation prompt.

Under the verbose protocol (a), HippoRAG 2 dominates every column (AC up to 74.1 vs. 56.0 for RAGU on BioASQ). This gap, however, is largely a format artifact: verbose answers mismatch the terse gold references, depressing both ROUGE-L (12 vs. 49) and Answer Correctness. Once format is controlled (b), the picture changes substantially. RAGU ties and slightly exceeds HippoRAG 2 on BioASQ AC (72.9 vs. 72.4) and closes the 2WikiMultiHopQA gap from −19.3 pp to −5.5 pp (58.0 vs. 63.5). HippoRAG 2 retains a genuine lead only on MuSiQue (54.4 vs. 40.1), the hardest multi-hop benchmark, where its personalized PageRank follows reasoning chains that consolidated retrieval does not surface—and where terseness even hurts the other systems’ Answer Correctness.

analysis.title: ToolAtlas overview: Memory Bootstrapping, Capability Exploration, and Dynamic Memory Traversal
analysis.summary: Paper page containing Figure 2, an overview of ToolAtlas. Stage 1, “Memory Bootstrapping,” turns Tool Info, Few-shot Examples, Real-world usage snippets, and Seed Tasks into verified Raw Trajectories through a Proposer and Executor; “Memory Induction” organizes these as an Agent-neutral Trace and a three-part Memory Architecture: Tool-Capability Graph G_cap, Tool-Strategy Graph G_strat, and trace graph G_trace. Stage 2, “Capability Exploration,” samples a local subgraph of G_cap, uses Known Capability to propose Boundary Task, Explore Capabilities, and Affordance Task probes, and writes verified outcomes back to memory. Stage 3, “Dynamic Memory Traversal,” uses read_trace(q), expand(q), read_strategy(q), and read_tool(T) actions to convert retrieved traces, tool entries, and strategies into Distilled Guidance for a User Agent and Final Answer. The surrounding text defines tool-node entry sets (U_i, B_i, C_i) for affordances, boundaries, and co-usage; explains Tool-Strategy Graph G_strat and cross-graph trace-tool and trace-strategy links; and begins Section 3.2, “Capability Exploration,” describing local-subgraph sampling and uncertainty-driven task proposals.
analysis.visible_text:
Figure 2: Overview of ToolAtlas. Stage 1 bootstraps a tool-side memory graph from seed tasks and verified rollouts, where Memory Induction converts raw trajectories into tool memory graph. Stage 2 uses the current graph to propose capability explorations that test tool boundaries and affordances, then writes verified outcomes back to the graph. Stage 3 traverses the graph at inference time and summarizes the retrieved traces, tool entries, and strategies into task-conditioned guidance for a user agent.

Tool-Capability Graph. Agent-neutral traces make rollouts reusable, but they are still organized by task. To support tool-side capability discovery, ToolAtlas builds a Tool-Capability Graph G_cap = (V_tool, E_tool) whose nodes are tools and whose inter-tool edges summarize recurrent co-usage patterns observed in agent-neutral traces. A tool node is connected to every trace node whose agent-neutral trace uses that tool, and we denote these trace-tool links by E_trace↔tool. These links let the tool node gather what related trace nodes reveal about the tool. Each tool node t_i carries three entry sets (U_i, B_i, C_i), where affordance entries U_i record valid uses that t_i reliably supports, boundary entries B_i mark regimes where t_i becomes unreliable or infeasible, and co-usage entries C_i document recurrent compositions with peer tools. This graph is the operational state used later for capability exploration. It tells the proposer what is already known about a tool and which affordances, boundaries, or compositions remain under-covered.

Tool-Strategy Graph. Some lessons are planning patterns rather than single-tool properties. Memory Induction captures them by grouping semantically related trace nodes or trace nodes with shared tool-use patterns, then distilling recurring task tips into strategy nodes. These nodes form the Tool-Strategy Graph G_strat = (V_strat, E_strat). We denote bidirectional trace-strategy links by E_trace↔strat. For example, file-system traces that first check allowed directories and locate the writable workspace can induce a strategy to discover the workspace and target scope before acting. This graph lets a user agent reuse high-level plans on similar tasks.

After Memory Induction, the complete tool memory graph consists of the three graphs, M_T = (G_trace, G_cap, G_strat) with cross-graph links E_trace↔tool between trace nodes and supported tool nodes, and E_trace↔strat between trace nodes and supported strategy nodes.

3.2 Capability Exploration

Memory Bootstrapping gives the MCP service an initial tool-side memory, but seed tasks still cover only a small region of the tool capability. Capability Exploration expands M_T by using the Tool-Capability graph as feedback. The graph records what is already known about each tool, and the task proposer uses that state to propose tasks that test what remains uncertain. At round r, ToolAtlas samples a local subgraph S^(r) of K related tools from the current Tool-Capability Graph G_cap^(r−1). The sampler starts from a target tool and follows co-usage edges, favoring plausible compositions.

regions.label: Figure 2 — Overview of ToolAtlas
regions.description: A three-stage system diagram. Memory Bootstrapping uses tool information and examples to brainstorm seed tasks, execute and verify rollouts, and induce a memory architecture from raw trajectories. Capability Exploration samples the Tool-Capability Graph to propose tasks targeting known capabilities, boundaries, and affordances, feeding verified findings back into memory. Dynamic Memory Traversal retrieves trace, strategy, tool, and neighboring-node information to produce distilled guidance for a user agent. A legend distinguishes forward flow, observed and uncovered affordances, and exploration of boundaries and affordances.
